prompt: A real long-lens telescope photograph of the Moon as a thin crescent with earthshine, high in a flat black sky, taken from airless ground with no atmosphere in between. Wide 16:9 frame. The Moon sits left of centre, its full circle about one quarter of the frame height across, its centre about one third down from the top edge and about one third in from the left edge. One hard, unfiltered sun from the far left: only a thin crescent along the left edge is sunlit, bright grey-white, about one eighth of the disc wide, the horns tapering to sharp points; along the terminator, crater rims and mountain peaks catch the light with hard black shadows falling to the right. The rest of the disc is lit only by earthshine, sunlight reflected from the Earth, which is out of frame: a very dim, dark charcoal grey, many times fainter than the crescent, where the darker maria are just barely readable as slightly darker patches and the bright ray crater Tycho and Aristarchus show as faint pale specks. The earthshine side has a crisp round edge against the sky and no glow around it. The sky: pure neutral black, an unexposed void, RGB zero, flat and identical from corner to corner, darker than the earthshine disc, with no gradient, no vignette, no colour cast and no lift toward the bottom; the bottom third of the frame is completely empty black where a horizon will be laid in later. No stars. Monochrome, neutral grey only. Finish: a real raw astrophotograph, sharp, fine grain, no gloss, no HDR look, no blobby painted maria. Match the raw grey finish and true black of the reference images, especially the long-lens half moon with the knife terminator, but this is a thin crescent with dim earthshine, not a half moon. No halo, no bloom, no glow around the crescent or the disc, no lens flare, no streaks, no text, no labels, no Earth in frame, no ground.

A real handheld photograph of the Earth taken through a spacecraft window with a long lens, in the manner of the Artemis II crew frames: a thin crescent Earth, high in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. The Earth sits in the upper left-centre of the frame, its full circle about one fifth of the frame width, the centre of the circle about one third down from the top edge. One hard, unfiltered sun from the far left: only the left edge of the globe is lit, as a thin crescent shaped like an opening bracket, about one sixth of the disc wide at its fattest, its two horns tapering to fine points above and below. The crescent is almost entirely cloud: dense bright white cloud fields, cloud streets and ragged storm edges, lit at a grazing angle so each cloud mass has a small hard shadow on its right side. Between the clouds only a few dark slate-blue gaps of ocean show; no land, no continents, no coastlines are readable. The terminator is hard and slightly ragged where tall cloud tops catch the last light past it, then the night side drops straight to black: the unlit part of the globe is exactly the same black as the sky, with no outline, no rim and no detail. Along the outer lit edge only, a single hairline of thin pale blue air, no wider than a pencil line, ending at the horns; it does not spread into the black. The sky: pure neutral black, an unexposed void, RGB zero, flat and identical from corner to corner, with no gradient, no vignette, no colour cast and no lift toward the bottom; the bottom third of the frame is completely empty black where a horizon will be laid in later. No stars at all, because the sunlit crescent sets the exposure. Finish: a raw camera file, fine sensor grain on the lit cloud only, slightly soft long-lens sharpness, no gloss, no ocean sun-glint, no saturation boost. This must not look like a CG globe or a painted planet. Match the raw grey spacecraft finish and true black of the reference images, but do not copy their subjects. No halo, no bloom, no glow beyond the hairline of blue air, no lens flare, no streaks, no reflections from the window, no text, no labels, no spacecraft parts, no horizon, no ground.

A raw black-and-white Cassini narrow-angle spacecraft frame of Hyperion, Saturn's small moon, alone in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. The moon is small: about one tenth of the frame width, placed in the upper right of the frame, its centre about one quarter down from the top edge and about one quarter in from the right edge; everything else is black. Hyperion is not round: an irregular, lumpy, potato-shaped rock, longer than it is wide, with a dented outline, its whole surface packed with deep, sharp-rimmed pits and craters so it looks like a pumice stone or a sponge. One hard, unfiltered sun from the far left: the left half of the moon is lit, light grey to off-white, the right half is lost in shadow, and the terminator is a hard, jagged, irregular line that follows the pits, with lit crater rims standing just past it on the dark side. Every pit on the lit side is filled with solid black shadow on its left wall and a lit right wall, all shadows falling to the right. The shadowed side is exactly the same black as the sky, with no outline and no detail. Monochrome only: greys on black, as an unprocessed probe image. The sky: pure neutral black, an unexposed void, RGB zero, flat and identical from corner to corner and edge to edge, no gradient, no vignette, no lift toward the bottom; the bottom third of the frame is completely empty black where a horizon will be laid in later. No stars, no Saturn, no other moons. Finish: a real spacecraft photograph, crisp, a little sensor grain on the lit surface only, slight raw-file softness at the very edge of the lit limb, no gloss. Match the raw grey finish and true black of the reference images, especially the half-lit moon with the knife terminator, but this body is small, irregular and sponge-like, not a round moon. No halo, no glow, no rim light, no lens flare, no streaks, no text, no labels, no ground.

A raw black-and-white Cassini wide-angle spacecraft frame of Saturn, with the rings open, high in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. Saturn sits right of centre, its globe about one fifth of the frame height across, its centre about one third down from the top edge; the whole ring system fits inside the frame with black space all round. The rings are tilted open about fifteen degrees, seen from slightly above the ring plane, as a long flat ellipse crossing in front of the lower half of the globe and passing behind its upper half. One hard, unfiltered sun from the far left: the globe is lit gibbous, its left side bright, a hard terminator curving down the right side and a thin crescent of the globe on the right in empty black. The proof of the light: the globe throws its shadow across the rings to its right, a hard-edged black wedge cutting clean through every ring band behind the planet, and the rings throw a thin dark shadow band across the globe just above where they pass in front of it. The rings are many nested ringlets of different widths and brightness, mid grey to near white, separated by sharp black gaps, with one wide black division (the Cassini Division) clearly open; the outer edge is crisp. The globe is smooth grey with faint horizontal cloud banding and no colour. Monochrome only: shades of grey on black, as an unprocessed clear-filter probe image. The sky: pure neutral black, an unexposed void, RGB zero, flat and identical from corner to corner and edge to edge, no gradient, no vignette, no grey veil, no lift toward the bottom or the lower left; the bottom third of the frame is completely empty black where a horizon will be laid in later. No stars, no moons. Finish: a real spacecraft photograph, sharp, slight sensor grain on the lit surfaces only, smooth tonal steps, no gloss, no rendered sheen. Match the finish and the true black of the reference images, especially the edge-on Saturn frame, but do not copy its edge-on geometry: here the rings are open. No halo or bloom on the limb, no lens flare, no streaks, no text, no labels, no arrows, no ground.
